claim: Approximately 10% of insect species are parasitoids.
source: It is estimated that approximately 10% of insect species are parasitoids, with females typically depositing their eggs either in (endoparasitoids) or on (ectoparasitoids) the bodies of their hosts, leading to the consumption of the host by the parasitoid's developing offspring (Eggleton and Belshaw, 1992; Vinson and Iwantsch, 1980; Charnov, 1994; Harvey and Strand, 2002; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; van de Kamp et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Eggleton and Belshaw, 1992; Vinson and Iwantsch, 1980; Charnov, 1994; Harvey and Strand, 2002; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; van de Kamp et al., 2018).

claim: Female parasitoids typically deposit their eggs either in (endoparasitoids) or on (ectoparasitoids) the bodies of their hosts.
source: It is estimated that approximately 10% of insect species are parasitoids, with females typically depositing their eggs either in (endoparasitoids) or on (ectoparasitoids) the bodies of their hosts, leading to the consumption of the host by the parasitoid's developing offspring (Eggleton and Belshaw, 1992; Vinson and Iwantsch, 1980; Charnov, 1994; Harvey and Strand, 2002; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; van de Kamp et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Eggleton and Belshaw, 1992; Vinson and Iwantsch, 1980; Charnov, 1994; Harvey and Strand, 2002; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; van de Kamp et al., 2018).

claim: Parasitoid development leads to the consumption of the host by the parasitoid's developing offspring.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Eggleton and Belshaw, 1992; Vinson and Iwantsch, 1980; Charnov, 1994; Harvey and Strand, 2002; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; van de Kamp et al., 2018).

claim: Drosophila suzukii originated in Asia.
source: This invasive species originated in Asia and has spread rapidly throughout the world over the last decade, with records in Europe (since 2008), North America (since 2008), South America (since 2013), and Africa (since 2017) (Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Boughdad et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Boughdad et al., 2021).

source: This invasive species originated in Asia and has spread rapidly throughout the world over the last decade, with records in Europe (since 2008), North America (since 2008), South America (since 2013), and Africa (since 2017) (Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Boughdad et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Boughdad et al., 2021).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Deprá et al., 2014; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Boughdad et al., 2021).

claim: Drosophila suzukii attacks a broad spectrum of soft-skinned fruits.
source: D. suzukii attacks a broad spectrum of soft-skinned fruits and causes serious economic damage to fruit and wine production (Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Asplen et al., 2015; Knapp et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Asplen et al., 2015; Knapp et al., 2021).

claim: Drosophila suzukii causes serious economic damage to fruit and wine production.
source: D. suzukii attacks a broad spectrum of soft-skinned fruits and causes serious economic damage to fruit and wine production (Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Asplen et al., 2015; Knapp et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Asplen et al., 2015; Knapp et al., 2021).

claim: Most well-recognized drosophilid parasitoids cannot parasitize D. suzukii.
source: Despite the broad interest in seeking natural enemies, the most well-recognized drosophilid parasitoids cannot parasitize D. suzukii (Chabert et al., 2012; Poyet et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Chabert et al., 2012; Poyet et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2019).

claim: Field investigations to identify natural parasitoids of D. suzukii were conducted from 2016-2020.
source: We conducted field investigations to identify natural parasitoids of D. suzukii from 2016–2020.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used in the study.

claim: Traps containing favourite fruits of D. suzukii were placed on Myrica rubra trees at several locations in East China.
source: We placed traps containing the favourite fruits of D. suzukii (e.g. banana pieces, cherries, and grapes) on Myrica rubra trees at several locations in East China (e.g. Hangzhou, Ningbo, and Taizhou), where D. suzukii is heavily distributed (Wang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used in the study, with citations supporting the distribution of D. suzukii (Wang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021).

claim: Trichopria drosophilae parasitizes D. suzukii pupae.
source: Among the reclaimed parasitic wasps, we primarily characterized two species: Trichopria drosophilae (Td) (Hymenoptera: Diapriidae), which parasitizes D. suzukii pupae, and Asobara japonica (Aj) (Braconidae), which parasitizes larvae.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the field investigations.

claim: Asobara japonica parasitizes D. suzukii larvae.
source: Among the reclaimed parasitic wasps, we primarily characterized two species: Trichopria drosophilae (Td) (Hymenoptera: Diapriidae), which parasitizes D. suzukii pupae, and Asobara japonica (Aj) (Braconidae), which parasitizes larvae.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the field investigations.

claim: The parasitic success of Td on D. suzukii has been documented in the USA and Europe.
source: The parasitic success of Td on D. suzukii has been documented in the USA and Europe independently (Knoll et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018b; Yi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Knoll et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018b; Yi et al., 2020).

claim: Td has evolved weaponized venom to help arrest host development.
source: By conducting an interdisciplinary study that integrates multi-omics analyses and functional behavioural assays, we found that, to adapt to the limited resources of the pupal host, this parasitoid has evolved weaponized venom and teratocyte cells to help arrest host development and speed up the digestion of host tissues.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from multi-omics analyses and functional behavioral assays conducted in the study.

claim: Td has evolved teratocyte cells to speed up the digestion of host tissues.
source: By conducting an interdisciplinary study that integrates multi-omics analyses and functional behavioural assays, we found that, to adapt to the limited resources of the pupal host, this parasitoid has evolved weaponized venom and teratocyte cells to help arrest host development and speed up the digestion of host tissues.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from multi-omics analyses and functional behavioral assays conducted in the study.

claim: Td allows intraspecific competition as a conditional collaboration to compensate for its inability to find younger hosts.
source: In addition, Td allowed intraspecific competition as a conditional collaboration to compensate for its inability to find more appropriate hosts (the younger ones) but effectively avoided interspecific competition with larval parasitoids.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from behavioral assays conducted in the study.

claim: Td effectively avoids interspecific competition with larval parasitoids.
source: In addition, Td allowed intraspecific competition as a conditional collaboration to compensate for its inability to find more appropriate hosts (the younger ones) but effectively avoided interspecific competition with larval parasitoids.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings from behavioral assays conducted in the study.

claim: Aj wasps mainly parasitize 2nd instar Drosophila larvae.
source: Aj wasps mainly parasitize 2nd instar Drosophila larvae, showing a 60% parasitism rate (the proportion of hosts parasitized) and a 48% emergence rate (the proportion of hosts with wasps hatched) on D. suzukii.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study.

claim: Aj shows a 60% parasitism rate on D. suzukii.
source: Aj wasps mainly parasitize 2nd instar Drosophila larvae, showing a 60% parasitism rate (the proportion of hosts parasitized) and a 48% emergence rate (the proportion of hosts with wasps hatched) on D. suzukii.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study.

claim: Aj shows a 48% emergence rate on D. suzukii.
source: Aj wasps mainly parasitize 2nd instar Drosophila larvae, showing a 60% parasitism rate (the proportion of hosts parasitized) and a 48% emergence rate (the proportion of hosts with wasps hatched) on D. suzukii.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study.

claim: Td laid eggs in the pupae.
source: In comparison to Aj, Td laid eggs in the pupae (Figure 1A) and presented a much better parasitic performance on D. suzukii, showing an 85% parasitism rate (p<0.001) and a 77% emergence rate (p<0.001) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Td shows an 85% parasitism rate on D. suzukii.
source: In comparison to Aj, Td laid eggs in the pupae (Figure 1A) and presented a much better parasitic performance on D. suzukii, showing an 85% parasitism rate (p<0.001) and a 77% emergence rate (p<0.001) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study, with reference to Figure 1B and C showing statistical significance (p<0.001).

claim: Td shows a 77% emergence rate on D. suzukii.
source: In comparison to Aj, Td laid eggs in the pupae (Figure 1A) and presented a much better parasitic performance on D. suzukii, showing an 85% parasitism rate (p<0.001) and a 77% emergence rate (p<0.001) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study, with reference to Figure 1B and C showing statistical significance (p<0.001).

claim: Td shows high parasitism rates in all tested Drosophila species, ranging from 80 to 89%.
source: Of these hosts, Td showed high parasitism rates in all species (ranging from 80 to 89%) and high emergence rates in most species (ranging from 73 to 79%), except in D. santomea (22%) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study, with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: Td shows high emergence rates in most tested Drosophila species, ranging from 73 to 79%, except in D. santomea (22%).
source: Of these hosts, Td showed high parasitism rates in all species (ranging from 80 to 89%) and high emergence rates in most species (ranging from 73 to 79%), except in D. santomea (22%) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the study, with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: Td is a generalist parasitoid with a wide host range, including D. suzukii and many other Drosophila species.
source: The parasitism spectrum in the laboratory showed that Td is also a generalist parasitoid with a wide host range, including D. suzukii and many other Drosophila species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parasitism efficiency data presented in the study.

claim: The assembled Td genome is 938.6 Mb.
source: We first sequenced and de novo assembled Td reference genome based on PacBio long reads (120.1 Gb). The assembled 938.6 Mb genome consisted of 1633 contigs with an N50 size of 146.9 Mb (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly results.

claim: The Td genome consists of 1633 contigs with an N50 size of 146.9 Mb.
source: We first sequenced and de novo assembled Td reference genome based on PacBio long reads (120.1 Gb). The assembled 938.6 Mb genome consisted of 1633 contigs with an N50 size of 146.9 Mb (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly results.

claim: BUSCO estimation showed a high level of completeness (96%) in terms of insect proteins for the Td genome.
source: BUSCO estimation showed a high level of completeness (96%) in terms of insect proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome quality assessment results.

claim: 97.8% of assembled contigs were anchored to six pseudochromosomes using Hi-C data.
source: By combining 143.7 Gb Hi-C data, 97.8% of assembled contigs were further anchored to six pseudochromosomes, agreeing with the karyotype staining estimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome assembly results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Td genome represents an occasionally large genome in parasitoids.
source: The assembled Td genome (938.6 Mb) represents an occasionally large one in parasitoids, since most published parasitoid and hymenopteran genomes were relatively small (<500 Mb) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the genome size data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Most published parasitoid and hymenopteran genomes were relatively small (<500 Mb).
source: The assembled Td genome (938.6 Mb) represents an occasionally large one in parasitoids, since most published parasitoid and hymenopteran genomes were relatively small (<500 Mb) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the genome size data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Parasitic lifestyle was previously assumed to be associated with reduced genome size and complexity.
source: Parasitic lifestyle was previously assumed to be associated with reduced genome size and complexity (Moran, 2002; Wicke et al., 2013; Poulin and Randhawa, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Moran, 2002; Wicke et al., 2013; Poulin and Randhawa, 2015).

claim: Ye et al. reported two large genomes (~950 Mb) of Anastatus parasitoids.
source: While this study was in preparation, Ye et al. reported two large genomes (~950 Mb) of Anastatus parasitoids (Chalcidoidae) and proposed that the unexpected genome expansion was due to recent bursts of long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons.
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Ye et al.

claim: Ye et al. proposed that the genome expansion in Anastatus was due to recent bursts of long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons.
source: While this study was in preparation, Ye et al. reported two large genomes (~950 Mb) of Anastatus parasitoids (Chalcidoidae) and proposed that the unexpected genome expansion was due to recent bursts of long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons.
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Ye et al.

claim: Recent bursts of transposon elements (TEs) were found in Td genome.
source: Similarly, we found recent bursts of transposon elements (TEs) in Td genome (Figure 1E), although a different class of TEs (DNA transposons, rather than LTRs) was the most abundant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the genome analysis, with reference to Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNA transposons, rather than LTRs, were the most abundant class of TEs in Td genome.
source: Similarly, we found recent bursts of transposon elements (TEs) in Td genome (Figure 1E), although a different class of TEs (DNA transposons, rather than LTRs) was the most abundant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the genome analysis, with reference to Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The age of the TE burst and the abundance of different classes both highly varied across parasitoid genomes, regardless of the whole genome size.
source: We further found that the age of the TE burst and the abundance of different classes both highly varied across parasitoid genomes, regardless of the whole genome size (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the comparative genome analysis, with reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ye et al. proposed that the expanded genome of Anastatus is stabilized owing to the expansion of the Piwi gene family.
source: The previous study has also proposed that the expanded genome of Anastatus is stabilized owing to the expansion of the Piwi gene family (Ye et al., 2022); however, Td genome only encodes three Piwi genes, which is similar to most other Hymenoptera species but much lower than those of Anastatus (16 and 30 genes).
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Ye et al., 2022.

claim: Td genome encodes three Piwi genes.
source: The previous study has also proposed that the expanded genome of Anastatus is stabilized owing to the expansion of the Piwi gene family (Ye et al., 2022); however, Td genome only encodes three Piwi genes, which is similar to most other Hymenoptera species but much lower than those of Anastatus (16 and 30 genes).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the genome annotation.

claim: Anastatus genomes encode 16 and 30 Piwi genes.
source: The previous study has also proposed that the expanded genome of Anastatus is stabilized owing to the expansion of the Piwi gene family (Ye et al., 2022); however, Td genome only encodes three Piwi genes, which is similar to most other Hymenoptera species but much lower than those of Anastatus (16 and 30 genes).
evidence: This is a reference to data from another study by Ye et al., 2022.

claim: The mechanisms to maintain the stability of genome size may vary between species.
source: These patterns suggest that the mechanisms to maintain the stability of genome size may vary between species and that the highly dynamic evolution of repeat contents has shaped great diversity across parasitoid genomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative genome analysis.

claim: The highly dynamic evolution of repeat contents has shaped great diversity across parasitoid genomes.
source: These patterns suggest that the mechanisms to maintain the stability of genome size may vary between species and that the highly dynamic evolution of repeat contents has shaped great diversity across parasitoid genomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative genome analysis.

claim: The official gene set for Td consists of 16,287 protein-coding genes.
source: By combining ab initio gene signatures, transcriptome evidence, and homologue alignments, we generated an official gene set consisting of 16,287 protein-coding genes for Td (Supplementary file 1; Methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genome annotation results.

claim: Td was placed as a sister sublineage to a large group of chalcid parasitoids with a divergence time of approximately 98 million years ago (Mya).
source: Td was placed as a sister sublineage to a large group of chalcid parasitoids with a divergence time of approximately 98 million years ago (Mya) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic analysis results, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The divergence of Td from Leptopilina dates back to 120 Mya.
source: Its divergence from Leptopilina, another major genus of drosophilid parasitoids (Cynipoidea), dates back to 120 Mya (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic analysis results, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Half of each parasitoid gene set consisted of universal genes across species.
source: Orthologue analysis showed that half of each parasitoid gene set consisted of universal genes across species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthologue analysis results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Approximately 83% of universal genes in Td experienced gene duplication events.
source: Interestingly, approximately 83% of universal genes in Td experienced gene duplication events.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orthologue analysis results.

claim: The gene family encoding tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs; IPR001820) was an extreme outlier in terms of expansion in Td.
source: By sorting all the expanded gene families within and between species, we found that the gene family encoding tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs; IPR001820) was an extreme outlier (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the gene family expansion analysis results, with reference to Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Td genome encodes 29 Timp genes.
source: Td genome encodes 29 Timp genes, much more than that of any other hymenopteran species (0–7 genes).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the gene family expansion analysis results.

claim: Other hymenopteran species encode 0-7 Timp genes.
source: Td genome encodes 29 Timp genes, much more than that of any other hymenopteran species (0–7 genes).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparative gene family analysis results.

claim: Timp gene copies in Td were located in 10 neighbouring regions of all Td chromosomes and formed three phylogenetic clades unique to Td.
source: These copies were located in 10 neighbouring regions of all Td chromosomes and formed three phylogenetic clades unique to Td, indicating multiple recent duplications (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genomic location and phylogenetic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2B and C.

claim: The genomic location and phylogenetic pattern of Timp genes indicate multiple recent duplications.
source: These copies were located in 10 neighbouring regions of all Td chromosomes and formed three phylogenetic clades unique to Td, indicating multiple recent duplications (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genomic location and phylogenetic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2B and C.

claim: Expression profiling of Timps showed widespread expression in most copies except for a unique sublineage that showed specialized expression in the venom glands.
source: Expression profiling of Timps showed widespread expression in most copies except for a unique sublineage that showed specialized expression in the venom glands (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the expression profiling results, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Td is a typical pupal parasitoid that lays eggs exclusively in the pupal stage of hosts.
source: Td is a typical pupal parasitoid that lays eggs exclusively in the pupal stage of hosts; adult wasps emerge from the host pupae after approximately 18 days at 25 °C (Figure 1A and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the life cycle of Td, with reference to Figure 1A and Figure 3A.

claim: Adult Td wasps emerge from the host pupae after approximately 18 days at 25 °C.
source: Td is a typical pupal parasitoid that lays eggs exclusively in the pupal stage of hosts; adult wasps emerge from the host pupae after approximately 18 days at 25 °C (Figure 1A and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the life cycle of Td, with reference to Figure 1A and Figure 3A.

claim: The pupal stage of D. suzukii and D. melanogaster normally lasts no longer than 5 days at 25 °C.
source: The pupal stage of the hosts is a non-feeding stage that normally lasts no longer than 5 days for D. suzukii and D. melanogaster at 25 °C.
evidence: This is a statement about the host biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Developmental arrest of the host is commonly observed in parasitized hosts.
source: One such adaptation is the consequent developmental arrest of the host, which is commonly observed in parasitized hosts (Rivers and Denlinger, 1995; Beckage and Gelman, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Rivers and Denlinger, 1995; Beckage and Gelman, 2004).

claim: Parasitized D. suzukii pupae showed evident defects in eye pigment deposition and bristle formation compared to non-parasitized pupae.
source: Compared to non-parasitized pupae, parasitized pupae showed evident defects in eye pigment deposition and bristle formation (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), strongly indicative of developmental arrest.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Phenotypic alterations in parasitized D. suzukii pupae started to occur on the second day post-parasitization.
source: These phenotypic alterations started to occur on the second day post-parasitization (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the development of the host pupae was immediately stopped after parasitization.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The development of the host pupae was immediately stopped after parasitization.
source: These phenotypic alterations started to occur on the second day post-parasitization (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the development of the host pupae was immediately stopped after parasitization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A similar pattern of developmental arrest was observed when D. melanogaster pupae were provided for parasitization.
source: We also performed parasitization experiments on another host species, D. melanogaster, for parallel comparisons and in-depth functional genetic investigations. Here, a similar pattern of developmental arrest was observed when D. melanogaster pupae were provided for parasitization (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Venom is the most likely effector resulting in host development arrest.
source: The most likely effector resulting in host development arrest is the venom, given that parasitoid wasps always inject venom into hosts along with oviposition to condition and manipulate the host for the successful development of wasp progeny (Werren et al., 2010; Asgari and Rivers, 2011; Moreau and Asgari, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about parasitoid biology, supported by citations (Werren et al., 2010; Asgari and Rivers, 2011; Moreau and Asgari, 2015).

claim: Venom injection at doses 1:20 and 1:40 markedly delayed the development of both D. suzukii and D. melanogaster hosts in comparison to the control.
source: As expected, doses 1:20 and 1:40 markedly delayed the development of both host species in comparison to the control (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The alternating effects of a higher dose of venom (1:20 dilution) were very similar to those parasitized by Td and stronger than those of the lower dose (1:40 dilution).
source: Moreover, the alternating effects of a higher dose of venom (1:20 dilution) were very similar to those parasitized by Td and stronger than those of the lower dose (1:40 dilution).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results.

claim: Td may arrest host development via the coinjection of venom.
source: Thus, our results suggest that Td may arrest host development via the coinjection of venom.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the venom injection experiments.

claim: 641 genes with solid expression evidence were characterized in Td venom glands.
source: To uncover the venom components that confer host developmental arrest, we sequenced the transcriptome of Td venom glands (VGs) and characterized 641 genes with solid expression evidence (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome sequencing results.

claim: 27 highly expressed venom proteins with known functions were characterized using LC‒MS/MS on Td venom.
source: Given that not all expressed genes are necessarily translated and secreted into the reservoir, we performed LC‒MS/MS on Td venom to further characterize reliable venom proteins (VPs) (Supplementary file 3). Of the 27 highly expressed (Z test, p<0.05) VPs with known functions, a pair of Timp genes with the highest expression values attracted the most attention (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proteomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: A pair of Timp genes (Timp1 and Timp2) with the highest expression values were identified among the venom proteins.
source: Of the 27 highly expressed (Z test, p<0.05) VPs with known functions, a pair of Timp genes with the highest expression values attracted the most attention (Figure 3D). Surprisingly, these two Timp genes were the previously highlighted Timp1 and Timp2 genes that showed expression specialization of venoms from the massive expansion in Td genome (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proteomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 3D and Figure 2.

claim: In insects, matrix metalloproteinases (Mmps) regulate pupal development by degrading extracellular matrix proteins.
source: In insects, matrix metalloproteinases (Mmps) regulate pupal development by degrading extracellular matrix proteins, and Timp delays pupal development (Jia et al., 2017; Jia and Li, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Jia et al., 2017; Jia and Li, 2023).

claim: Timp delays pupal development in insects.
source: In insects, matrix metalloproteinases (Mmps) regulate pupal development by degrading extracellular matrix proteins, and Timp delays pupal development (Jia et al., 2017; Jia and Li, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Jia et al., 2017; Jia and Li, 2023).

claim: The development of D. melanogaster pupae was markedly delayed upon the expression of DmTimp.
source: As expected, the development of D. melanogaster pupae was markedly delayed upon the expression of DmTimp (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Ectopic expression of either TdTimp1 or TdTimp2 did not lead to a visible developmental delay.
source: Although ectopic expression of either TdTimp1 or TdTimp2 did not lead to a visible developmental delay, driving the expression of both TdTimp1 and TdTimp2 arrested the development of D. melanogaster as effectively as the expression of DmTimp (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Driving the expression of both TdTimp1 and TdTimp2 arrested the development of D. melanogaster as effectively as the expression of DmTimp.
source: Although ectopic expression of either TdTimp1 or TdTimp2 did not lead to a visible developmental delay, driving the expression of both TdTimp1 and TdTimp2 arrested the development of D. melanogaster as effectively as the expression of DmTimp (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Cocktails of TdTimp1 and TdTimp2 are bioactive compounds of the venom that result in host development arrest.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that cocktails of TdTimp1 and TdTimp2 are bioactive compounds of the venom that result in host development arrest.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: Td released a special group of cells into the host haemocoel along with egg hatching.
source: We found that as host development was arrested, Td simultaneously released a special group of cells into the host haemocoel along with egg hatching (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 100 cells were secreted into the host haemocoel after larval hatching.
source: Approximately 100 cells were secreted into the host haemocoel after larval hatching (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The cell number remained constant during the first three days, then decreased drastically, and finally vanished on day 8.
source: The cell number remained constant during the first three days, then decreased drastically, and finally vanished on day 8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A); that is, these cells no longer divided after being released.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: These cells no longer divided after being released.
source: The cell number remained constant during the first three days, then decreased drastically, and finally vanished on day 8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A); that is, these cells no longer divided after being released.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that cell numbers remained constant initially, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: These cells rapidly grew, with initially 85±13 µm in diameter and up to approximately 249±57 µm before vanishment.
source: Moreover, these cells rapidly grew, with initially 85±13 µm in diameter and up to approximately 249±57 µm before vanishment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: These characteristics agree with those of teratocytes found in other parasitoids.
source: These characteristics agree with those of teratocytes found in other parasitoids (Hotta et al., 2001; Pedata et al., 2003; Firlej et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Hotta et al., 2001; Pedata et al., 2003; Firlej et al., 2007).

claim: These cells are defined as teratocytes, which is the first discovery of teratocytes in the family Diapriidae.
source: Thus, we defined these cells as teratocytes, which is the first discovery of teratocytes in the family Diapriidae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and comparison with other parasitoids.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy of Td teratocytes revealed a dense lawn of microvilli on the cell surface.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of Td teratocytes revealed a dense lawn of microvilli on the cell surface and that each cell consisted of a spherical nucleus, substantial amounts of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Each Td teratocyte consisted of a spherical nucleus, substantial amounts of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of Td teratocytes revealed a dense lawn of microvilli on the cell surface and that each cell consisted of a spherical nucleus, substantial amounts of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: These features indicate high levels of protein synthesis and secretory activity in Td teratocytes.
source: These features indicate high levels of protein synthesis and secretory activity in Td teratocytes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electron microscopy observations.

claim: Host tissues incubated with teratocytes from a single parasitoid were partially digested at 12 hr and fully digested after 30 hr.
source: Compared with the control, which was maintained for 30 hr without digestion, host tissues incubated with teratocytes from a single parasitoid were partially digested at 12 hr and fully digested after 30 hr (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Teratocytes facilitate the effective dissociation of host tissues.
source: These findings suggest that teratocytes facilitate the effective dissociation of host tissues, which may play a key role in nutritional exploitation for parasitoid larvae development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro coculture experiments.

claim: Teratocytes may play a key role in nutritional exploitation for parasitoid larvae development.
source: These findings suggest that teratocytes facilitate the effective dissociation of host tissues, which may play a key role in nutritional exploitation for parasitoid larvae development.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the in vitro coculture experiments.

claim: A total of 3784 genes were expressed in teratocytes.
source: We further conducted transcriptomic profiling to characterize the teratocyte genes that facilitate host tissue digestion. A total of 3784 genes were expressed in teratocytes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome sequencing results.

claim: The majority of the 129 genes with significantly high expression in teratocytes were ribosome- (48 genes) and digestion-related genes (23 genes).
source: The majority of the 129 genes with significantly high expression (Z-test, p<0.05) were ribosome- (48 genes) and digestion-related genes (23 genes) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Eight trypsin genes dominated among the highly expressed digestion-related genes in teratocytes.
source: Eight trypsin genes dominated among the highly expressed digestion-related genes in teratocytes, indicating their essential role in digesting host tissues.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results.

claim: Trypsin genes play an essential role in digesting host tissues.
source: Eight trypsin genes dominated among the highly expressed digestion-related genes in teratocytes, indicating their essential role in digesting host tissues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptome analysis results.

claim: Trypsin is the most abundant proteinase in invertebrate digestive systems.
source: Trypsin is the most abundant proteinase in invertebrate digestive systems (Muhlia-Almazán et al., 2008; Dias et al., 2015; Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Muhlia-Almazán et al., 2008; Dias et al., 2015; Shao et al., 2021).

claim: Along with the increase in trypsin inhibitor concentration, the digestion of host tissues was gradually inhibited.
source: Along with the increase in inhibitor concentration, we found that the digestion of host tissues was gradually inhibited (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Applying a trypsin inhibitor resulted in significantly lower emergence rates of parasitoid wasps, especially upon the injection of higher amounts of inhibitors.
source: As expected, applying a trypsin inhibitor resulted in significantly lower emergence rates of parasitoid wasps, especially upon the injection of higher amounts of inhibitors (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Trypsin inhibitor injection led to abnormal wasp larvae development.
source: Correspondingly, we noticed that the trypsin inhibitor injection led to abnormal wasp larvae development.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations.

claim: Upon injection of 400 ng TLCK per host, the parasitoid larvae were found to be significantly smaller than the control on day 4 and almost dead on day 6 post-parasitization.
source: Upon injection of 400 ng TLCK per host, the parasitoid larvae were found to be significantly smaller than the control on day 4 and almost dead on day 6 post-parasitization, owing to the lack of well-digested food (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Teratocytes degrade host tissues using digestive enzymes, such as trypsin, to provide essential nutrients for the development and survival of wasps.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that teratocytes degrade host tissues using digestive enzymes, such as trypsin, to provide essential nutrients for the development and survival of wasps.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trypsin inhibitor experiments.

claim: Td fed old host pupae (4-day-old) showed a dramatic reduction in both parasitism rate and wasp emergence rate.
source: By testing the parasitism efficiency in host pupae of different ages (1- to 4-day-old D. suzukii or D. melanogaster), we found that Td fed old host pupae (4-day-old) showed a dramatic reduction in both parasitism rate and wasp emergence rate (p<0.001) (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Both male and female wasps that emerged from young hosts (1-day-old) exhibited larger body sizes than those that emerged from old pupae.
source: Simultaneously, both male and female wasps that emerged from young hosts (1-day-old) exhibited larger body sizes than those that emerged from old pupae (Student's t-test, p<0.001) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ovaries and VGs of females that emerged from young hosts were significantly larger than those from old hosts.
source: We further found that the ovaries and VGs of females that emerged from young hosts were significantly larger than those from old hosts (p<0.001) (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Significantly more mature eggs were found from females that emerged from young host pupae.
source: By dissecting the ovaries, we found significantly more mature eggs from females that emerged from young host pupae (p<0.001, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The parasitization of young hosts benefits the fitness of Td.
source: These results showed that the parasitization of young hosts benefits the fitness of Td.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parasitism efficiency and fitness measurements.

claim: Td wasps showed no significant preference for either young or old host pupae.
source: Regardless of whether the choice lasted for 2 or 4 hr, Td wasps showed no significant preference for either young or old host pupae (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Td wasps have not evolved the ability to discriminate the young host pupae as a priority for parasitization.
source: These results indicate that Td wasps have not evolved the ability to discriminate the young host pupae as a priority for parasitization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oviposition choice assays.

claim: Both the parasitism and emergence rates were significantly improved by superparasitism.
source: To test this hypothesis, we evaluated the parasitic efficiency of hosts with multiple infections. Strikingly, both the parasitism and emergence rates were significantly improved by superparasitism (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5A and B.

claim: The resulting benefit of superparasitism was particularly evident in parasitizing old pupae (4-day-old), in which low parasitic efficiencies by monoparasitism were recovered 2.2-fold (parasitism rate) and 3.2-fold (emergence rate) by superparasitism.
source: The resulting benefit was particularly evident in parasitizing old pupae (4-day-old), in which low parasitic efficiencies by monoparasitism were recovered 2.2-fold (parasitism rate) and 3.2-fold (emergence rate) by superparasitism (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 5A and B.

claim: Only one adult Td emerged from the superparasitized pupae.
source: Despite the better parasitization performance, we noted that only one adult Td emerged from the superparasitized pupae.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations.

claim: Superparasitism likely leads to the additional introduction of venom and teratocytes, which maximizes the utilization of host nutrition, especially in older hosts with poorer resources.
source: Superparasitism likely leads to the additional introduction of venom and teratocytes, which maximizes the utilization of host nutrition, especially in older hosts with poorer resources.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Superparasitism in Td may partially compensate for the inability to recognize young pupae as hosts.
source: Therefore, superparasitism in Td may partially compensate for the inability to recognize young pupae as hosts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the superparasitism experiments.

claim: Td wasps used their ovipositors to sting Aj-parasitized host pupae, similar to what they did for non-parasitized pupae.
source: We found that Td wasps used their ovipositors to sting Aj-parasitized host pupae, similar to what they did for non-parasitized pupae.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental observations.

claim: Almost no eggs were laid inside Aj-parasitized Td-stung pupae, in contrast to the high oviposition rate (approximately 93% for both Drosophila hosts) of non-Aj-parasitized pupae.
source: However, almost no eggs were laid inside these Aj-parasitized Td-stung pupae, in contrast to the high oviposition rate (approximately 93% for both Drosophila hosts) of non-Aj-parasitized pupae (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental results, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Td could discriminate between larva-parasitized hosts to avoid competition with larval parasitoids.
source: Thus, Td could discriminate between larva-parasitized hosts to avoid competition with larval parasitoids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the interspecific competition assays.

claim: The ovipositor stylet had two types of sensilla on its dorsal and ventral valves: the surface-dome and the coeloconic sensilla.
source: Using scanning electron microscopy, we found that the ovipositor stylet had two types of sensilla on its dorsal and ventral valves: the surface-dome and the coeloconic sensilla (Figure 6D–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 6D–I.

claim: Coeloconic sensilla was the most abundant type on the ovipositor stylet.
source: Coeloconic sensilla was the most abundant type, and secretory pores and surface-dome sensilla were also found on Td ovipositor stylets (Figure 6F–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 6F–I.

claim: Secretory pores and surface-dome sensilla were also found on Td ovipositor stylets.
source: Coeloconic sensilla was the most abundant type, and secretory pores and surface-dome sensilla were also found on Td ovipositor stylets (Figure 6F–I).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 6F–I.

claim: These sensilla and secretory pores occurred on the distal end of the ovipositor stylet but not on the proximal end.
source: These sensilla and secretory pores occurred on the distal end of the ovipositor stylet but not on the proximal end, and there were more sensilla and secretory pores on the dorsal valve than on the ventral valve (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 6D–F.

claim: There were more sensilla and secretory pores on the dorsal valve than on the ventral valve.
source: These sensilla and secretory pores occurred on the distal end of the ovipositor stylet but not on the proximal end, and there were more sensilla and secretory pores on the dorsal valve than on the ventral valve (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electron microscopy observations, with reference to Figure 6D–F.

claim: These anatomical features support a possible role of the ovipositor stylet in host discrimination.
source: These anatomical features support a possible role of the ovipositor stylet in host discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electron microscopy observations.

claim: Principal component analysis placed the ovipositor closer to the antennae and legs of both males and females.
source: Based on the overall expression profiles, principal component analysis placed the ovipositor closer to the antennae and legs of both males and females (Figure 6J), indicating a strong functional correlation among these anatomically non-contact organs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 6J.

claim: There is a strong functional correlation among the ovipositor, antennae, and legs.
source: Based on the overall expression profiles, principal component analysis placed the ovipositor closer to the antennae and legs of both males and females (Figure 6J), indicating a strong functional correlation among these anatomically non-contact organs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the principal component analysis results, with reference to Figure 6J.

claim: Three chemosensory protein genes (CSPs) and two odourant-binding protein genes (OBPs) showed extremely high expression in both ovipositors and female antennae.
source: By further comparing the expression profiles of ovipositors and female antennae, we found that three chemosensory protein genes (CSPs) and two odourant-binding protein genes (OBPs) showed extremely high expression in both tissues, as well as a few genes encoding gustatory receptors (GRs) and olfactory receptors (ORs) (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 6K.

claim: The general co-receptor, Orco, does not express in the ovipositor.
source: More interestingly, the general co-receptor, Orco, which forms heteromultimeric complexes with other ligand-selective ORs, does not express in the ovipositor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and most genes related to odourant reception (i.e. OBPs and other ORs) showed biased expression in the antennae, while most taste recognition-related genes, i.e., GRs and CSPs, were more highly expressed in the ovipositor (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6K.

claim: Most genes related to odourant reception (i.e. OBPs and other ORs) showed biased expression in the antennae.
source: More interestingly, the general co-receptor, Orco, which forms heteromultimeric complexes with other ligand-selective ORs, does not express in the ovipositor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and most genes related to odourant reception (i.e. OBPs and other ORs) showed biased expression in the antennae, while most taste recognition-related genes, i.e., GRs and CSPs, were more highly expressed in the ovipositor (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 6K.

claim: Most taste recognition-related genes, i.e., GRs and CSPs, were more highly expressed in the ovipositor.
source: More interestingly, the general co-receptor, Orco, which forms heteromultimeric complexes with other ligand-selective ORs, does not express in the ovipositor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and most genes related to odourant reception (i.e. OBPs and other ORs) showed biased expression in the antennae, while most taste recognition-related genes, i.e., GRs and CSPs, were more highly expressed in the ovipositor (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 6K.

claim: A few GRs with the highest expression in ovipositors were found.
source: Correspondingly, we found a few GRs with the highest expression in ovipositors (Figure 7; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the transcriptome analysis results, with reference to Figure 7 and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Td ovipositors are more likely to serve as taste organs by sensing contact signals inside the host pupae for host discrimination.
source: These patterns further support the hypothesis that, unlike the antennae that confer odourant chemoreception, Td ovipositors are more likely to serve as taste organs by sensing contact signals inside the host pupae for host discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptome analysis results.

claim: Many koinobiont parasitoids that attack early host periods (e.g. larvae) maintain hosts alive and growing for sustained resource availability.
source: Many koinobiont parasitoids that attack early host periods (e.g. larvae) maintain hosts alive and growing for sustained resource availability (Brodeur and Boivin, 2004; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006), while certain idiobiont parasitoids that usually attack non-feeding host stages (e.g. pupae) alternatively arrests host development for high-quality resources.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Brodeur and Boivin, 2004; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006).

claim: Certain idiobiont parasitoids that usually attack non-feeding host stages (e.g. pupae) alternatively arrest host development for high-quality resources.
source: Many koinobiont parasitoids that attack early host periods (e.g. larvae) maintain hosts alive and growing for sustained resource availability (Brodeur and Boivin, 2004; Pennacchio and Strand, 2006), while certain idiobiont parasitoids that usually attack non-feeding host stages (e.g. pupae) alternatively arrests host development for high-quality resources.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about parasitoid biology.

claim: Immune suppressors and virulence proteins dominate the VPs of Leptopilina larval parasitoids.
source: For example, previous studies have shown that immune suppressors and virulence proteins dominate the VPs of Leptopilina larval parasitoids (Colinet et al., 2011; Colinet et al., 2013; Poirié et al., 2014; Heavner et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research (Colinet et al., 2011; Colinet et al., 2013; Poirié et al., 2014; Heavner et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2021).

claim: Td uses venom to arrest host pupal development and maintain young status via the recruitment of Timps.
source: Td uses venom to arrest host pupal development and maintain young status via the recruitment of Timps (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Td released teratocytes to accelerate the digestion of host tissues.
source: Moreover, Td released a special type of cell along with egg hatching, teratocytes, to accelerate the digestion of host tissues (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The functional integration benefits Td as the utilization of nutritional resources is highly efficient during a limited period.
source: The functional integration benefits Td as the utilization of nutritional resources is highly efficient during a limited period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The adaptations adopted by pupal parasitoids are largely unique to those of larval parasitoids and highly associated with the non-feeding and relatively inactive conditions of pupae.
source: The adaptations adopted by pupal parasitoids are largely unique to those of larval parasitoids and highly associated with the non-feeding and relatively inactive conditions of pupae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of parasitoid strategies.

claim: Few characterized genes of parasitic effectors in Td were related to immune responses.
source: Correspondingly, few characterized genes of these parasitic effectors were related to immune responses (Supplementary file 3 and 4), indicating that conflict with host immunity plays a minor role in the adaptation of pupal parasitoids.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the gene annotation results.

claim: Conflict with host immunity plays a minor role in the adaptation of pupal parasitoids.
source: Correspondingly, few characterized genes of these parasitic effectors were related to immune responses (Supplementary file 3 and 4), indicating that conflict with host immunity plays a minor role in the adaptation of pupal parasitoids.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene annotation results.

claim: It was proposed that the co-option of single-copy genes plays a common role in recruiting venom genes in certain parasitoids, such as Nasonia.
source: Although it was proposed that the co-option of single-copy genes plays a common role in recruiting venom genes in certain parasitoids, such as Nasonia (Martinson et al., 2017), specific cases have also been reported highlighting gene duplication events, including duplicated Lar in the venom of a generalist L. heterotoma that suppresses host immune responses and the massive expansion of Warm in L. boulardi, which helps the specialist parasitoid evade host immune attacks (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Martinson et al., 2017.

claim: Specific cases have been reported highlighting gene duplication events, including duplicated Lar in the venom of a generalist L. heterotoma that suppresses host immune responses.
source: Although it was proposed that the co-option of single-copy genes plays a common role in recruiting venom genes in certain parasitoids, such as Nasonia (Martinson et al., 2017), specific cases have also been reported highlighting gene duplication events, including duplicated Lar in the venom of a generalist L. heterotoma that suppresses host immune responses and the massive expansion of Warm in L. boulardi, which helps the specialist parasitoid evade host immune attacks (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Huang et al., 2021.

claim: The massive expansion of Warm in L. boulardi helps the specialist parasitoid evade host immune attacks.
source: Although it was proposed that the co-option of single-copy genes plays a common role in recruiting venom genes in certain parasitoids, such as Nasonia (Martinson et al., 2017), specific cases have also been reported highlighting gene duplication events, including duplicated Lar in the venom of a generalist L. heterotoma that suppresses host immune responses and the massive expansion of Warm in L. boulardi, which helps the specialist parasitoid evade host immune attacks (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a reference to another study by Huang et al., 2021.

claim: These differences suggest a highly diverse evolutionary mode of parasitism across different genera.
source: These differences suggest a highly diverse evolutionary mode of parasitism across different genera.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative analysis of parasitoid strategies.

claim: Timps as a major compound in the venom confer host developmental arrest.
source: In this study, we characterized Timps as a major compound in the venom that confers host developmental arrest (Figure 3), trypsin as a major component in teratocytes that facilitates host digestion (Figure 4), and a set of chemoreception proteins recruited by ovipositors for taste recognition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Trypsin as a major component in teratocytes facilitates host digestion.
source: In this study, we characterized Timps as a major compound in the venom that confers host developmental arrest (Figure 3), trypsin as a major component in teratocytes that facilitates host digestion (Figure 4), and a set of chemoreception proteins recruited by ovipositors for taste recognition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: A set of chemoreception proteins recruited by ovipositors for taste recognition.
source: In this study, we characterized Timps as a major compound in the venom that confers host developmental arrest (Figure 3), trypsin as a major component in teratocytes that facilitates host digestion (Figure 4), and a set of chemoreception proteins recruited by ovipositors for taste recognition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: All affected genes (Timps, trypsins, and chemoreception proteins) were found to have undergone massive duplication events.
source: Strikingly, all affected genes were found to have undergone massive duplication events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene family analysis.

claim: Timp gene family was mainly present in holometabolous insects such as Diptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, and Hymenoptera.
source: By searching for Timps across insects, we found that this gene family was mainly present in holometabolous insects such as Diptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, and Hymenoptera (Figure 2C), possibly because of its role in regulating metamorphosis in this class of insects.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparative genomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Timp gene family is possibly present in holometabolous insects because of its role in regulating metamorphosis in this class of insects.
source: By searching for Timps across insects, we found that this gene family was mainly present in holometabolous insects such as Diptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, and Hymenoptera (Figure 2C), possibly because of its role in regulating metamorphosis in this class of insects.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the comparative genomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The massive expansion of Timps in Td was derived from three independent phylogenetic sublineages.
source: The massive expansion of Timps in Td was derived from three independent phylogenetic sublineages, including one clustered with other hymenopteran copies, one clustered with patchy copies inside the clade of other insect orders, and one that is relatively unique (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The third sublineage is of the most expansion, in which most components were located on chromosome 6 and showed widespread expression across most tissues and developmental stages.
source: The third sublineage is of the most expansion, in which most components were located on chromosome 6 and showed widespread expression across most tissues and developmental stages (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genomic location and expression profiling results, with reference to Figure 2B and D.

claim: The two VP genes (TdTimp1 and TdTimp2) that confer host development arrest were derived from tandem duplication of the third sublineage and further experienced expression specialization in venom.
source: The two VP genes (TdTimp1 and TdTimp2) that confer host development arrest were derived from tandem duplication of this sublineage and further experienced expression specialization in venom.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genomic location, phylogenetic, and expression profiling results.

claim: Another four copies of the third sublineage possibly translocated to other chromosomes, showing expression specialization in larvae and teratocytes.
source: We noted another four copies of this sublineage that possibly translocated to other chromosomes, showing expression specialization in larvae and teratocytes (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genomic location and expression profiling results, with reference to Figure 2B and D.

claim: A few GRs originated from tandem duplications and experienced an expression shift to the ovipositor.
source: Similarly, we found that a few GRs originated from tandem duplications and experienced an expression shift to the ovipositor (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genomic location and expression profiling results, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Gene expression shift, followed by gene expansion, may play a common role in the unique functional adaptations of Td.
source: Thus, we propose that gene expression, followed by gene expansion, may play a common role in the unique functional adaptations of Td.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene family and expression analysis.

claim: Superparasitism usually lowers the reproductive efficiency of parasitoids by affecting their development, resulting in premature mortality of both hosts and parasitoids.
